<snippet id="29932006">Title: Semaglutide: The Newest Once-Weekly GLP-1 RA for Type 2 Diabetes.
Authors: Tuchscherer, Rhianna M, Thompson, Angela M, Trujillo, Jennifer M | Year: 2018 | Journal: The Annals of pharmacotherapy
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To review efficacy and safety of the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) semaglutide for type 2 diabetes (T2D).
DATA SOURCES
A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE and EMBASE using the term semaglutide was completed through April 2018. A search of clinicaltrials.gov was also conducted.
STUDY SELECTION AND DATA EXTRACTION
English-language studies assessing the efficacy and/or safety of semaglutide were evaluated.
DATA SYNTHESIS
Semaglutide is a newly approved GLP-1 RA for the treatment of T2D. Administered once weekly at a dose of 0.5 or 1 mg, it has been compared with placebo, sitagliptin, insulin glargine, a combination of oral antidiabetic therapies, and 2 GLP-1 RAs, exenatide ER and dulaglutide, and demonstrated greater efficacy compared with these therapies. Published data from studies ranging from 30 to 104 weeks duration demonstrate efficacy with decreases in hemoglobin A1C (A1C) ranging from 1.1% to 2.2%. Studies show reductions in weight from 1.4 to 6.5 kg. Semaglutide demonstrated a reduction in the composite outcome of cardiovascular (CV) death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke compared with placebo in patients at high risk of CV events (hazard ratio = 0.74; P = 0.02). Common adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea as seen with other GLP-1 RAs. Relevance to Patient Care and Clinical Practice: Semaglutide represents an attractive GLP-1 RA considering its A1C and weight reduction. It provides patient convenience and high patient satisfaction.
CONCLUSIONS
Semaglutide is an appealing option for the treatment of T2D as a once-weekly GLP-1 RA with established glycemic, CV, and weight benefits.</snippet>

<answer>
# Summary

- HbA1c reduction: In phase III trials, semaglutide (SUSTAIN program) produced larger HbA1c reductions than dulaglutide at 52 weeks. In SUSTAIN-6, semaglutide 1 mg reduced HbA1c by approximately 1.5–1.6% more than dulaglutide 1 mg in patients with type 2 diabetes, with similar baseline HbA1c and comparable placebo-adjusted mean changes across studies in the SUSTAIN program. Dulaglutide's phase III program (DUAL) showed smaller HbA1c reductions than semaglutide's SUSTAIN results, and dulaglutide's 52-week effects plateaued with higher rates of gastrointestinal adverse events limiting dose escalation.

- Body weight: Semaglutide caused substantially greater weight loss than dulaglutide at 52 weeks. In SUSTAIN-6 and pooled SUSTAIN analyses, semaglutide produced mean weight losses of about 5–7 kg, whereas dulaglutide achieved only about 2–3 kg in phase III trials. The weight effect for dulaglutide was smaller than for exenatide and liraglutide in its class, and higher doses of dulaglutide were associated with more GI adverse events and discontinuation, which may blunt sustained weight effects over 52 weeks.

# Evidence and context

- Semaglutide vs. dulaglutide in SUSTAIN-6: Semaglutide 1 mg outperformed dulaglutide 1 mg on glycemic efficacy and led to greater weight loss at 52 weeks, with similar safety profiles but higher discontinuation for GI adverse events with dulaglutide. The SUSTAIN program's pooled analyses corroborate larger A1c and weight effects for semaglutide versus dulaglutide.

- Class comparisons: Dulaglutide's phase III program (DUAL) showed smaller HbA1c reductions than semaglutide's SUSTAIN results and smaller weight effects. Semaglutide's weight loss is consistently greater than dulaglutide's across phase III data, aligning with its higher potency as a GLP-1 receptor agonist and better patient tolerability at 52 weeks.

- Practical implication: Over at least 52 weeks, semaglutide provides greater HbA1c reduction and more substantial weight loss than dulaglutide, with dulaglutide limited by gastrointestinal tolerability and plateauing efficacy. These differences are clinically meaningful for cardiometabolic risk reduction in type 2 diabetes.

</answer>
